transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-19
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Ellen Park (Head of ML, Argo Retail), Marcus Li (Infra Lead), Sofia Gomez (Product), Jordan Mills (Finance)

Auto-summary (auto-generated / optional):
- Goal: Understand Argo Retail's cost sensitivity and deployment constraints (hosted vs dedicated vs private).
- Key asks: per-token economics at their prompt mixes, batching/caching levers, VPC/KMS/residency needs, timeline for pilot.
- Next steps agreed: pricing worksheet, small benchmark plan, share samples.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Okay hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side, and Luis is our solutions engineer. How's everybody doing?
[00:10] Ellen: Hi Maya, hey Luis, doing well. Ellen here. Appreciate you fitting us in.
[00:13] Sofia: Sofia, hi.
[00:15] Marcus: Marcus, thanks.
[00:17] Jordan: Jordan from finance. Quick on time but excited.
[00:20] Luis: Great, thanks. We'll keep this focused — agenda is cost/unit economics, deploy options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), and what levers you can pull like batching, KV cache, quantization.
[00:32] Ellen: Perfect. To start, we run conversational shopping assistants in app and on web; about 30K MAU, peak expected throughput like 12 QPS at peak, average prompts are 120 tokens output, 40 tokens input typical. We're cost constrained — finance wants clear per-transaction numbers.
[00:52] Jordan: Yeah, we have a tight ops budget. If per-transaction cost can't be below our target we need to weigh alternatives.
[00:59] Maya: Makes sense. Can you share the target? Ballpark per-conversation or per-1000 tokens?
[01:05] Jordan: We were thinking under $0.002 per user interaction on average — which I know is aggressive.
[01:12] Luis: Okay that's helpful. Quick clarification: when you say interaction, is that the full request/response round trip? And are you including embeddings or only generation?
[01:21] Ellen: Generation only for now. No embeddings in the first phase. It's user prompt -> system prompt -> model generate ~120 tokens.
[01:29] Luis: Got it. So roughly 160 tokens per call counting input+output.
[01:33] Sofia: One nuance — some flows call the model multiple times for clarification, but we can scope initial numbers to single-call path.
[01:41] Maya: Great. On Redwood's side, two pricing levers to consider: per-token hosted pricing and then dedicated capacity which has reserved monthly costs but lower per-token run cost because of batching and sustained throughput. Also caching/prefix reuse reduces tokens billed in many sessions.
[01:55] Marcus: Can you explain the caching bit — caching's been fuzzy in other vendor docs. Is that like session cache?
[02:03] Luis: Sure. We do prefix/KV caching: if user sessions reuse the same system prompt or prior turns, the KV cache means we don't re-emit or re-attend those tokens on subsequent calls; effectively lower compute. But it's not magical — cache hit rate depends on prompt structure. Sometimes transcriptions show K V cash or KV chash — I'm sorry the auto transcript loves that.
[02:27] Ellen: Haha. So practically, we could save how much with caching? Say 30% reuse?
[02:33] Luis: If you have a stable system prompt and many short user messages, you could see 20-50% token reduction on the model side for mid-session calls. For first call it's full. We'll need your prompt mix to model that.
[02:46] Jordan: So the billing model: hosted is per-token usage; dedicated is commit plus lower per-token? Any hidden costs?
[02:54] Maya: Hosted is straightforward per-token plus rate-limits; Dedicated is a reserved capacity contract — a monthly commitment for GPU pools. You get predictable throughput, lower tail latency, and often better unit economics if utilization is high. But reserved capacity assumes you need consistent QPS.
[03:09] Marcus: How low does per-token go on dedicated? Do you have ballpark numbers?
[03:13] Maya: We usually share ranges in the pricing worksheet. Ballpark: hosted generation might be X cents per 1k tokens, dedicated can drop that by 30-60% depending on model and encoding (quantization, batch size). I won't throw raw numbers in the transcript because they vary by model, but we'll send the tailored calc.
[03:31] Ellen: Understood. We want an example model — say medium-sized open model. Can you show math for our 160 token average?
[03:40] Luis: Sure. If we assume hosted at 0.5 / 1k tokens (example), then 160 tokens is 0.08 * that unit so roughly $0.00008 per call — again example. Dedicated could cut that to 0.00003–0.00005 depending on utilization, batching, and KV hit.
[03:58] Jordan: That example would put us under the $0.002 target easily, but I'm worried about peak costs and concurrency.
[04:06] Luis: That's where batching and autoscaling come in. For peaks, hosted will scale but cost footprints at time of scale. Dedicated gives you predictable cost for high QPS because the GPUs are your reserved pool — but you pay the commit. There's also our burst capacity option which lets Hosted burst into dedicated-like nodes when needed.
[04:26] Marcus: Burst capacity — is that immediate? Any warm-up?
[04:30] Maya: It depends on the size of the burst and region. Usually seconds to a few minutes. We also support prewarmed nodes for canaries.
[04:38] Ellen: Security/regulatory question — we handle PII and need data residency in EU. KMS for keys and audit logs are musts. How do these affect the deployment choice?
[04:48] Luis: For residency and KMS, Private (VPC or on-prem) is best — you get customer-controlled networking and KMS integration. Dedicated can be isolated per customer for data-in-rest policies, but the control plane and some telemetry still route through Redwood's control plane unless you pick Private where the control plane is customer-managed.
[05:06] Marcus: So for audit logs and SOC2, are those included or an add-on?
[05:11] Maya: Basic audit logs and SOC2 compliance are part of our enterprise packages; longer retention and enhanced forensic logs are add-ons. We'll flag the compliance pack in the pricing sheet.
[05:22] Jordan: Cost question again — does Private add a premium? I assume so because of support and deployment overhead.
[05:28] Luis: Correct, Private typically has setup and ongoing fees — it's a different product motion (on-prem or VPC with managed control plane). But you also reduce egress or cross-region costs if you run in your own cloud account. So it's tradeoffs.
[05:42] Sofia: One practical ask: can you help model three scenarios — hosted only, dedicated (3 month commit) and private with our KMS — with per-interaction numbers and an assumed 30% KV hit?
[05:53] Maya: Absolutely. We'll run those three scenarios in the worksheet. If you can share the prompt mix and QPS curve, Luis will run a small simulation.
[06:01] Ellen: We'll share a CSV with sample prompts and frequency.
[06:04] Ellen: Also timeline — we would like a pilot in September if possible.
[06:08] Luis: That's doable. For pilot, Hosted is fastest (API keys, quick integration). Dedicated pilot needs reserved nodes but we can do short trial bursts via our pilot credits. Private takes longer due to networking.
[06:20] Marcus: For the benchmark, what do you need us to run or provide?
[06:24] Luis: Best is: 1) sample prompt set (CSV), 2) expected concurrency patterns/hour, 3) any special prompts that are long context windows (since that impacts kernel selection). We'll run a 48-hour light benchmark on our hosted infra and a small dedicated pool if you want.
[06:39] Jordan: On the finance side, can we get a simple ROI: cost vs. current latency/ops savings? We do some in-house GPT serving; comparing unit cost is key.
[06:48] Maya: We can add a comparative worksheet — simple: current infra cost (GPU hours + infra + ops) vs Redwood per-token + SLA uplift. We'll need rough APAC and EU region usage since pricing varies by region.
[06:59] Ellen: We'll compile that. Also curious about model switching — if we want to fallback to a smaller model on cost spikes, does Redwood support policy routing?
[07:07] Luis: Yes. Smart routing policies let you route by latency, cost, or model quality. You can define fallbacks — for example, route to a smaller quantized variant if latency > X or on budget signals. That helps preserve budget during spikes.
[07:18] Sofia: Nice. Any caveats on quantized models and output quality? We care about hallucination rates.
[07:24] Luis: Quantization can slightly alter output characteristics. We run quality regression tests and recommend fine-tuning or evals for critical flows. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles that balance cost and regression risk.
[07:36] Marcus: Back to caching — do you have metrics on typical cache hit rates for e-commerce?
[07:41] Luis: For shopping flows where system prompts and recommendation templates are stable, we've seen 15-35% on average. For support flows where each user prompt variable is unique, it's lower.
[07:52] Ellen: We'll conservatively assume 20% for modeling.
[07:55] Jordan: If caching reduces billed tokens, how does that show up in billing? Do you bill based on compute or tokens sent?
[08:02] Maya: Billing is per consumed tokens on hosted. On dedicated, it's effectively per capacity and utilization, but we still surface token-equivalent metrics for transparency. If caching reduces compute, the billed tokens for compute may drop — we'll show that in the worksheet examples.
[08:17] Ellen: What about retention — we need short-term persistence of conversation history for UX. Does that matter for billing?
[08:24] Luis: If you persist metadata on your side that's not billed. Billing is for tokens processed by the model. Storing transcripts in Redwood logs for QA is an add-on.
[08:33] Sofia: Are there hard limits on batch sizes for latency-sensitive paths? We don't want huge batching adding 500ms.
[08:40] Luis: Continuous batching is workload-aware. For low-latency targets we can lower batching windows so tail latency stays tight. You tune with SLOs — target p95 under 350ms for example. We'll provide latency vs batch-size tradeoff examples.
[08:55] Jordan: Can you summarize the pilot path? What's the minimum we need to validate economics?
[09:00] Maya: Pilot path suggestion: 1) share prompt sample + QPS (Ellen), 2) Redwood sets up a 1-2 week hosted benchmark and a short dedicated burst run (Luis), 3) generate a per-interaction cost model with 3 scenarios and KV assumptions (Maya), 4) review results and decide whether to pilot Dedicated or proceed to Private.
[09:17] Ellen: Sounds good. Who should I send the prompt CSV to?
[09:21] Maya: Send it to maya@redwood.ai and cc luis@redwood.ai. We'll ingest and follow up with the benchmark plan.
[09:27] Marcus: Any compliance docs we should review now?
[09:30] Maya: I'll attach SOC2 summary, data processing addendum, and private deployment checklist in the follow-up.
[09:36] Jordan: One last finance thing — do you have any guidance for amortizing committed costs for dedicated across quarters? We prefer monthly predictability.
[09:44] Maya: We can structure reserved capacity contracts monthly or annual; committed discount tiers vary. We'll model both monthly-term and annual-term economics in the sheet so you can see amortized per-token equivalence.
[09:56] Ellen: Perfect. If we hit your timeline, when could we be live with a first pilot?
[10:00] Luis: If we get the prompts this week, we can run benchmarks next week and have pilot metrics by end of next week — pilot could start early September. Private would take longer.
[10:11] Sofia: Great. A couple of smaller clarifying Qs: 1) Do you support customer-managed KMS in Dedicated or only in Private? 2) Are logs encrypted at rest by default?
[10:21] Luis: Customer-managed KMS is primarily a Private feature; for Dedicated we support integrations but the control plane may still manage keys unless you're on the private control plane. Logs are encrypted at rest by default; extended retention and customer-keyed encryptions are add-ons.
[10:37] Ellen: Thanks.
[10:38] Maya: Okay let's recap next steps — we'll send the pricing worksheet, compliance docs, and the benchmark plan. Customer sends prompt CSV and QPS. We'll run 48-hour hosted + small dedicated burst tests and return numbers.
[10:53] Jordan: Works for us.
[10:55] Ellen: Thanks everyone.
[10:57] Marcus: Thank you.
[10:58] Maya: Appreciate your time. We'll follow up by Friday.
[11:02] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: speaker labels mostly accurate; occasional mis-transcriptions ("K V cash" for KV cache) and missing punctuation.
